Two divergences are recorded rather than resolved: the reading surfaced a condition the review does not list, a prohibition on a pending felony charge in another jurisdiction, and did not surface the life-sentence exclusion that both the review and the internal reference state. The life-sentence point is returned as a release blocker rather than decided against counsel on a single reading. Second, the forms. Edition 1.2 in fact retains seven New York assets and reading them closes all three: the Notice of Motion and Affidavit in Support of Sealing under CPL § 160.59; a CPL § 160.59 pro se sealing application packet with instructions; the Criminal Certificate of Disposition request form at REV-2024-07; a request for CPL § 160.59 seal verification; the Office of Court Administration's application to destroy a marijuana conviction record; a Local Criminal Record Search request at REV-2024-04; and a youthful offender determination application. The discretionary sealing petition is therefore buildable end to end, from the Certificate of Disposition request the review says to build first through to post-grant verification. Assembly Bill A10951 (2025-2026) was read at the New York State Senate's bill channel on 2026-08-06: it makes technical corrections to the Clean Slate law on multicategory conviction dockets and the conviction-specific supervision prohibitor, it would broaden that prohibitor from supervision "for the conviction eligible for sealing" to any probation or parole supervision, and it sits in the Assembly Codes Committee with its last action a referral to codes on April 14, 2026. Destruction is therefore conditional on a participant-signed request rather than automatic, which the review does not say and which this memo previously recorded the other way; the marijuana route is restructured accordingly and nothing else is. tracks.legalName: Sealing of a Case Terminated in the Defendant's Favour (CPL § 160.50)
tracks.publicName: Your New York case that ended in your favor should already be sealed

controllingAuthority.summary: Where a criminal action terminates in the defendant's favour — a dismissal, an acquittal, a declination to prosecute, an adjournment in contemplation of dismissal that is then dismissed, or a vacated or overturned conviction — the record is sealed by direction of the court at disposition. There is no waiting period, no application and nothing to file. New York seals; it does not expunge, except for the marijuana destruction remedy. A sealed record does not appear on background checks run by employers, housing providers and other non-law-enforcement entities, and the person may generally answer that they have no criminal record. Sealed records remain accessible to law enforcement, prosecutors and courts in a new criminal case; to entities permitted or required to run fingerprint-based background checks for work with children, the elderly and people with disabilities; to entities mandated by law to consider sealed records; to the New York State Education Department for hiring, discipline and licensing; to private transportation network companies; to police and peace officer employers; and for firearms licensing. Federal and immigration authorities may also reach them, and a sealed conviction still counts as a predicate for sentence enhancement in a later case. New York sealing reaches New York State records only.

exclusions: An adjournment in contemplation of dismissal that has not yet been dismissed. The ACD period must run first.
Federal and out-of-state records.
Cases where the prosecutor moved successfully to keep the record unsealed in the interests of justice. The scope of that motion is recorded below as an open question.

tracks.legalName: Clean Slate Automatic Sealing of Criminal Convictions (CPL § 160.57(1)(b))

controllingAuthority.summary: Eligible New York convictions are sealed automatically, with nothing filed. A misdemeanour seals when at least three years have passed from the defendant's release from incarceration, or from the imposition of sentence if there was no sentence of incarceration; a felony seals when at least eight years have passed from the date the defendant was last released from incarceration for the sentence of the conviction eligible for sealing, or from the imposition of sentence if there was no incarceration. If the defendant is subsequently convicted of a crime before a prior conviction is sealed, the calculation of time for that prior conviction starts on the same date as the calculation for the subsequent conviction: a re-anchoring rule, not a pause. Every condition must be satisfied, including that the defendant is not currently under the supervision of any probation or parole department for the conviction eligible for sealing, that no subsequent criminal charge is pending in this state, that the conviction is not for an offence defined as a sex offence or sexually violent offence under Correction Law § 168-a, and that it is not a class A felony, except that class A felony offences defined in Penal Law article 220 are carved back in. New York seals; it does not expunge, except for the marijuana destruction remedy. A sealed record does not appear on background checks run by employers, housing providers and other non-law-enforcement entities, and the person may generally answer that they have no criminal record. Sealed records remain accessible to law enforcement, prosecutors and courts in a new criminal case; to entities permitted or required to run fingerprint-based background checks for work with children, the elderly and people with disabilities; to entities mandated by law to consider sealed records; to the New York State Education Department for hiring, discipline and licensing; to private transportation network companies; to police and peace officer employers; and for firearms licensing. Federal and immigration authorities may also reach them, and a sealed conviction still counts as a predicate for sentence enhancement in a later case. New York sealing reaches New York State records only.

exclusions: Convictions for an offence defined as a sex offence or a sexually violent offence under Correction Law § 168-a.

Class A felony convictions, except class A felony offences defined in Penal Law article 220, which are carved back in. This is the opposite of the CPL § 160.59 list, which excludes all class A felonies including drug felonies.
Any conviction where the defendant is currently under the supervision of a probation or parole department for that conviction.
Any conviction where a subsequent criminal charge is pending in New York.
Federal and out-of-state convictions, which New York sealing does not reach.

controllingAuthority.summary: Convictions for the marijuana offences described in CPL § 160.50(3)(k) are vacated, dismissed and expunged by operation of law under § 160.50(5)(a). That stage is automatic: there is no waiting period, no motion, no fee and nothing for the participant to file, and under § 160.50(5)(b)(i) the chief administrator of the courts notifies the Division of Criminal Justice Services and the heads of all appropriate police departments, district attorneys' offices and other law enforcement agencies, who mark the records as expunged. Destruction is a second and distinct stage and is not automatic: § 160.50(5)(b)(i) provides that upon the written request of the individual whose case has been expunged, or their designated agent, such records shall be destroyed, and the Office of Court Administration publishes an application for that request. Section 160.50(5)(b)(ii) describes what the subdivision requires as automatic vacatur, dismissal and expungement including record destruction if requested, which places the participant's request inside the same statutory mechanism rather than beside it. This is the only true erasure in New York; every other track seals. Expunged marijuana convictions do not count toward the two-conviction limit on the discretionary sealing petition, which can move a participant from ineligible to eligible there. The Marihuana Regulation and Taxation Act chapter-law citation is still not pinned and the review cites the Act generically rather than to a section.

That this is the only true erasure in New York, and that every other New York remedy seals rather than destroys. The distinction is the single most important thing to keep right in consumer copy. legalDesignDecision.rationale: One relief mechanism under CPL § 160.50(5), normalized as a sequential composition rather than as pure guidance. The route was carrying a participant-signed official form inside a no-filing guidance classification: component ny_mrta_marijuana-destruction-request-instructions-2 declared official_pdf_fill and MRTA-DESTRUCTION-REQUEST on a track whose own strategy was process_guidance, and the manual-completion item for it was the participant signing and sending it. A participant-signed, participant-submitted official instrument cannot sit inside a route classified as having no participant filing. Reading CPL § 160.50 at the New York State Senate's published-statutes channel on 2026-08-07 settles the structure and corrects the framing the review left open. Paragraph (5)(a) vacates, dismisses and expunges by operation of law. Paragraph (5)(b)(i) then provides that upon the written request of the individual whose case has been expunged, or their designated agent, such records shall be destroyed. Destruction is therefore not automatic, and the request is not a way to confirm or chase relief the State already gave: it is the sole statutory trigger for a distinct legal effect. Paragraph (5)(b)(ii) places that request inside the same statutory architecture in the statute's own words, describing what the subdivision requires as automatic vacatur, dismissal and expungement including record destruction if requested. That makes this a composed relief mechanism and not a supporting action. The statute creates two legally distinct stages with different actors: at the first the chief administrator of the courts notifies the record holders and the participant does nothing, and at the second the individual or their designated agent makes a written request and the holders destroy. The conditional relationship is legally meaningful, because only the individual whose case has been expunged may make the request, so the second unit presupposes the first. And the request is not a correction or follow-up for a failed automatic process: the statute supplies a separate route for that at § 160.50(5)(b)(ii)(B). A supporting_action node would have had to assert that the automatic process did not occur, which is not this route's premise and which the design must not claim. Both units seek relief under the same subdivision on the same record, so no second relief track is created and no second remedy is offered for relief the State already granted. The automatic stage stays guidance and stays first, no participant filing is generated for it, and the destruction request is produced only where the participant asks for it. What remains open is the Marihuana Regulation and Taxation Act chapter-law citation and the current content of § 160.50(3)(k), the revision and official publication of the retained application, and the procedure around the request.

units.label: The automatic vacatur, dismissal and expungement, and how to check it
units.description: The default stage, and the one that runs first. Under CPL § 160.50(5)(a) a conviction for an offence described in § 160.50(3)(k) is vacated and dismissed and all records of it expunged, by operation of law. Nothing is filed, no motion is made, no fee is charged and the participant does nothing to obtain it: under § 160.50(5)(b)(i) the chief administrator of the courts notifies the Division of Criminal Justice Services and the heads of all appropriate police departments, district attorneys' offices and other law enforcement agencies, and those holders mark the record as expunged. No participant filing exists at this stage and none is generated. The guidance explains what expungement means, that the courts do not send a notice when it happens, how to check through a DCJS Record Review, why an absence in that report is consistent with expungement rather than proof of destruction, and the separate § 160.50(5)(b)(ii)(B) route where court records cannot be located or the expungement has not been reflected. Where the participant wants nothing beyond expungement, the route ends here.

units.label: Participant-signed request that the expunged records be destroyed
units.description: The conditional stage, reached only where the participant asks for destruction. It is not a chase of a failed automatic process and does not assert that anything went wrong: destruction is simply never automatic. CPL § 160.50(5)(b)(i) provides that upon the written request of the individual whose case has been expunged, or their designated agent, such records shall be destroyed, and § 160.50(5)(b)(ii) describes what the subdivision requires as automatic vacatur, dismissal and expungement including record destruction if requested. The request is therefore a conditional unit of the same statutory mechanism rather than a second remedy, and its precondition is that the case has already been expunged. The instrument is the Office of Court Administration's application to destroy a marijuana conviction record, retained in Edition 1.2 at MRTA-DESTRUCTION-REQUEST, which the participant signs, dates and sends to the Office of Court Administration rather than filing in a court. LegalEase prepares the participant's portion from their own answers; it does not certify eligibility, does not certify that the expungement occurred, does not advise whether to ask for destruction and does not submit the request. The unit is never offered at the outset.

controllingAuthority.summary: CPL § 160.57(1)(a), read at the New York State Senate's published-statutes channel on 2026-08-06, provides that convictions for subdivision one of Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1192 shall be sealed after three years. This is a traffic infraction rather than a crime; it sits in its own paragraph with its own three-year period, and the paragraph does not on its face carry the paragraph (b) conditions on pending charges, supervision status, sex offences and class A felonies. Whether those conditions nonetheless apply, and what event starts the three years, are the central open questions on this track. Nothing is filed. New York seals; it does not expunge, except for the marijuana destruction remedy. Sealed records remain accessible to law enforcement, prosecutors and courts in a new criminal case; to entities running fingerprint-based checks for work with children, the elderly and people with disabilities; to entities mandated by law to consider them; to the New York State Education Department; to private transportation network companies; to police and peace officer employers; and for firearms licensing. Federal and immigration authorities may also reach them, and a sealed conviction still counts as a predicate for sentence enhancement. New York sealing reaches New York State records only.

tracks.publicName: Petition to seal your New York convictions

controllingAuthority.summary: A person with up to two convictions, of which no more than one may be a felony, may petition the court of conviction to seal them at least ten years after sentencing or release, whichever is later, with time spent incarcerated after the target conviction extending the clock by an equivalent period. Crimes arising from a single criminal transaction may be treated as one conviction, and expunged marijuana convictions do not count toward the limit. There must be no open or pending criminal charges. An eligible offence is any New York crime except sex offences under Penal Law article 130 and offences requiring sex offender registration under Correction Law article 6-C, child pornography and sexual performance offences under article 263, felony homicide offences under article 125, violent felony offences as defined in Penal Law § 70.02, class A felonies, and felony conspiracy or attempt where the target offence is itself ineligible. Note the difference from Clean Slate: all class A felonies are excluded here, including article 220 drug felonies that Clean Slate carves back in. Relief is discretionary and the court weighs rehabilitation and the interests of justice. New York seals; it does not expunge, except for the marijuana destruction remedy. Sealed records remain accessible to law enforcement, prosecutors and courts in a new criminal case; to entities running fingerprint-based checks for work with children, the elderly and people with disabilities; to entities mandated by law to consider them; to the New York State Education Department; to private transportation network companies; to police and peace officer employers; and for firearms licensing. Federal and immigration authorities may also reach them, and under CPL § 160.59(10) a sealed conviction remains a predicate for sentence enhancement in a later case. New York sealing reaches New York State records only.
